\section*{AP \({ }^{\text {® }}\) CALCULUS AB \\ 2007 SCORING GUIDELINES (Form B)}

\section*{Question 6}

Let \(f\) be a twice-differentiable function such that \(f(2)=5\) and \(f(5)=2\). Let \(g\) be the function given by \(g(x)=f(f(x))\).
\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] Explain why there must be a value \(c\) for \(2<c<5\) such that \(f^{\prime}(c)=-1\).
\item[(b)] Show that \(g^{\prime}(2)=g^{\prime}(5)\). Use this result to explain why there must be a value \(k\) for \(2<k<5\) such that \(g^{\prime \prime}(k)=0\).
\item[(c)] Show that if \(f^{\prime \prime}(x)=0\) for all \(x\), then the graph of \(g\) does not have a point of inflection.
\item[(d)] Let \(h(x)=f(x)-x\). Explain why there must be a value \(r\) for \(2<r<5\) such that \(h(r)=0\).
\item[(a)] The Mean Value Theorem guarantees that there is a value \(c\), with \(2<c<5\), so that
\[
f^{\prime}(c)=\frac{f(5)-f(2)}{5-2}=\frac{2-5}{5-2}=-1 .
\]
\item[(b)] \(\quad g^{\prime}(x)=f^{\prime}(f(x)) \cdot f^{\prime}(x)\)
\[
\begin{aligned}
& g^{\prime}(2)=f^{\prime}(f(2)) \cdot f^{\prime}(2)=f^{\prime}(5) \cdot f^{\prime}(2) \\
& g^{\prime}(5)=f^{\prime}(f(5)) \cdot f^{\prime}(5)=f^{\prime}(2) \cdot f^{\prime}(5)
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus, \(g^{\prime}(2)=g^{\prime}(5)\).
Since \(f\) is twice-differentiable, \(g^{\prime}\) is differentiable
everywhere, so the Mean Value Theorem applied to \(g^{\prime}\) on [2, 5] guarantees there is a value \(k\), with \(2<k<5\), such that \(g^{\prime \prime}(k)=\frac{g^{\prime}(5)-g^{\prime}(2)}{5-2}=0\).
\item[(c)] \(g^{\prime \prime}(x)=f^{\prime \prime}(f(x)) \cdot f^{\prime}(x) \cdot f^{\prime}(x)+f^{\prime}(f(x)) \cdot f^{\prime \prime}(x)\)
If \(f^{\prime \prime}(x)=0\) for all \(x\), then
\(g^{\prime \prime}(x)=0 \cdot f^{\prime}(x) \cdot f^{\prime}(x)+f^{\prime}(f(x)) \cdot 0=0\) for all \(x\).
Thus, there is no \(x\)-value at which \(g^{\prime \prime}(x)\) changes sign, so the graph of \(g\) has no inflection points.
OR
If \(f^{\prime \prime}(x)=0\) for all \(x\), then \(f\) is linear, so \(g=f \circ f\) is linear and the graph of \(g\) has no inflection points.
\end{itemize}
\(2:\left\{\begin{array}{l}1: \frac{f(5)-f(2)}{5-2} \\ 1: \text { conclusion, using MVT }\end{array}\right.\)
\[
3:\left\{\begin{array}{l}
1: g^{\prime}(x) \\
1: g^{\prime}(2)=f^{\prime}(5) \cdot f^{\prime}(2)=g^{\prime}(5) \\
1: \text { uses MVT with } g^{\prime}
\end{array}\right.
\]
\(2:\left\{\begin{array}{l}1: \text { considers } g^{\prime \prime} \\ 1: g^{\prime \prime}(x)=0 \text { for all } x\end{array}\right.\)
OR
\(2:\left\{\begin{array}{l}1: f \text { is linear } \\ 1: g \text { is linear }\end{array}\right.\)
\(2:\left\{\begin{array}{l}1: h(2) \text { and } h(5) \\ 1: \text { conclusion, using IVT }\end{array}\right.\)
\begin{itemize}
\item[(d)] Let \(h(x)=f(x)-x\).
\[
\begin{aligned}
& h(2)=f(2)-2=5-2=3 \\
& h(5)=f(5)-5=2-5=-3
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(h(2)>0>h(5)\), the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees that there is a value \(r\), with \(2<r<5\), such that \(h(r)=0\).
\end{itemize}
